newsitem.title: FRANCE: Crippled Frenchman writes book with wink of an eye.
newsitem.headline: Crippled Frenchman writes book with wink of an eye.

text.p: A French journalist who was paralysed and made mute by disease dictated a 150-page book, letter by letter, by winking his left eye, his publisher said on Thursday.

Jean-Dominique Bauby winked to signal the right letter as a copywriter from publishers Robert Laffont went through the alphabet for months to take down "Le Scaphandre et le Papillon" (The Diving Suit and the Butterfly).

Bauby has been lying motionless in hospital in the Channel resort of Berck since suffering a heart attack 15 months ago. The attack left him paralysed except for his left eye, but his intellect was untouched.
Copywriter Claude Mendibil said she spent six hours a day with Bauby taking down the text he had endlessly repeated in his head.
"Jean-Dominique moved his left eyelid some 200,000 times," she told the weekly Paris Match.
As their communication code improved, Bauby, in his 30s, went from dictating half a page a day to almost three pages a day.
Bauby winked once for 'yes' and twice for 'no'. Mendibil read out the letters in the order of those most frequently used in the French language.

"I felt Jean-Dominique needed to get rid of an excess of words from his memory. I had to free him from all that text as quickly as possible. I admit that in the beginning it was terrible," Mendibil said.
She said they had problems with the penultimate of the 29 chapters, which Bauby entitled in English "A Day in the Life".
For example, as he dictated "pur pleonasme" (pure pleonasm), she believed he was dictating in English "purple eonasm".
In the book, due out on Thursday, Bauby described his life in hospital with humour.

According to one excerpt published by Paris Match, he said there were two kinds of people in the hospital: those who were attentive to his distress signals, and the others -- "like this friendly idiot who switched off the (televised) Bordeaux-Munich soccer game at half-time with an irrevocable 'Good Night'.
